problem.title: Design a URL Shortener
problem.prompt: Design a URL shortening service similar to bit.ly or TinyURL. Users submit a long URL and receive a short alias (e.g., https://short.ly/aB3xY). When a user visits the short URL, the service redirects them to the original. The service must handle high read traffic, provide low-latency redirects, and allow optional analytics per short URL.

learningJourney.title: Why URL shortener scale is a read-cache and alias-allocation problem
learningJourney.explanation: With `100M` new URLs/day (`~1,160` writes/sec) and a `100:1` read-to-write ratio (`~116,000` redirects/sec, peaking higher on viral links), a URL shortener is overwhelmingly read-heavy. Aliases must be compact (`7` Base62 chars = `62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion` combinations), collision-free, and redirect in `< 10 ms` p99.

learningJourney.title: What happens with hash collisions and synchronous analytics
learningJourney.explanation:
Two design mistakes cripple URL shorteners under viral traffic:

1. **Synchronous Click DB Updates**: Incrementing `UPDATE urls SET clicks = clicks + 1` on every redirect turns a `116k QPS` read workload into `116k QPS` of row-locked DB writes.
2. **MD5 Truncation Collisions**: Truncating an MD5/SHA256 hash to 7 chars forces a DB `SELECT` + retry loop on every write and leaks predictability.

learningJourney.title: Naive solution (and why auto-increment IDs or MD5 truncation fail)
learningJourney.explanation:
A naive implementation uses a single Postgres `SERIAL` column encoded to Base62 or truncates `md5(long_url)[:7]`:

- **Single DB Bottleneck**: One auto-increment sequence cannot scale writes multi-region and exposes sequential enumeration.
- **Hash Retry Loops**: Truncated hashes collide under the birthday paradox, requiring DB round-trips to verify uniqueness.
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Naive solution under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Range-Allocated Base62 Keys + Redis Redirects + Kafka Analytics
learningJourney.explanation:
Production URL shorteners decouple key generation, redirects, and analytics:

- **Collision-Free Key Generation**: Each API server leases a non-overlapping numeric range (e.g., `1,000,000` IDs from ZooKeeper/etcd) or uses a distributed Snowflake/Feistel-scrambled counter encoded in **Base62** (`[a-zA-Z0-9]`), guaranteeing zero collisions with zero DB checks.
- **Custom Aliases & Expiry**: Store `(short_alias, long_url, expires_at)` in a sharded KV/DB partitioned by `hash(short_alias)`.
- **Low-Latency Redirects**: Lookup `short_alias` in Redis (`< 2 ms`), return `302 Found` (or `301` when analytics aren't needed), and emit click telemetry asynchronously to Kafka.

sectionDiagram.title: Range-Based Base62 Minting vs. Cached 302 Redirect
sectionDiagram.summary: Local counter ranges eliminate write-path collision checks, while Redis + async Kafka keep redirect latency < 10 ms.

learningJourney.title: Where URL Shortener Patterns apply in System Design
learningJourney.explanation:
The range-allocated Base62 + read-cache pattern powers many high-read indirection systems:

- **Link Shorteners & QR Code Platforms (Bitly)**: Global edge caching with asynchronous clickstream aggregation.
- **Pastebins & Shareable Permalinks**: Generating unguessable, collision-free short keys without DB round-trips.
- **Affiliate & Ad Tracking Redirectors**: Sub-10 ms `302` redirects paired with Kafka click attribution.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should a URL shortener emit click events asynchronously to Kafka instead of updating a click counter in the database during the redirect?

options.text: Synchronous DB counter updates turn a 100:1 read-heavy redirect path into row-locked write contention, breaking the < 10 ms p99 SLA
options.feedback: Correct: decoupling analytics via Kafka keeps the redirect path fast and lock-free.

options.text: Because Base62 aliases cannot be stored in a relational database
options.feedback: Base62 aliases are stored in the database; the issue is synchronous write contention on every read.

options.text: Because HTTP 302 redirects forbid database access
options.feedback: HTTP 302 doesn't forbid DB access, but synchronous writes hurt tail latency.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
